There is a particular hour before the rest of the house wakes when the kitchen belongs only to me. I fill the kettle, and the sound of water against stainless steel is oddly ceremonial. Outside, the sky is still deciding what color it wants to be. Some mornings it is the blue of old denim; others, a pale apricot that makes the bare branches look like ink drawings.

I used to rush through this ritual, treating coffee as fuel, not as a moment. But somewhere along the way I began to notice that the first sip tastes different when I have watched the steam curl upward without checking my phone. It is warmer, more deliberate. The bitterness is not an insult but an anchor.

There is a kind of freedom in allowing your attention to be small. We are told constantly to think big, to optimize, to scale our lives. But a patch of sunlight moving across the floor does not want to be optimized. It only wants to be seen.

So I lean against the counter and hold the warm mug with both hands. The clock ticks. A bird begins its uneven song. For a few minutes, I am not behind on anything. I am not a list of tasks. I am just a person in a kitchen, watching the day arrive slowly, like a letter slipped under the door. No urgency, no audience, just the simple fact of being present. And somehow that is enough.
